column1: Is this new story proof in physics that MOND is finished? Https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/technology/is-dark-matter-s-main-rival-theory-dead-the-cassini-spacecraft-and-other-recent-tests-may-invalidate-mond/ar-BB1maqMN?ocid=hpmsn&cvid=31541f6e52e74450 The question of whether MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) is “finished” is a complex one, and the answer depends on how one interprets the evidence. MOND was proposed as an alternative to dark matter, suggesting that the observed discrepancies in galactic rotation curves could be explained by modifying the laws of gravity at low accelerations, rather than invoking unseen matter. However, the recent findings from the Cassini spacecraft and other tests have cast significant doubt on MOND’s ability to account for all observed phenomena.   The Cassini data, in particular, provides a stringent test of gravitational theories. By precisely measuring the spacecraft’s trajectory during its mission to Saturn, scientists were able to test predictions of both general relativity and MOND in the weak-field regime. The results align closely with general relativity, leaving little room for MOND to explain the observed effects without introducing additional ad hoc assumptions. This is not the first time MOND has faced challenges—earlier observations of galaxy clusters and the cosmic microwave background have also posed difficulties for the theory.   That said, it’s important to note that MOND is not a monolithic theory. There are various formulations, some of which attempt to incorporate relativistic effects or additional fields to address these challenges. However, these modifications often complicate the theory, reducing its initial appeal as a simpler alternative to dark matter. Moreover, the success of the Lambda-CDM model, which incorporates dark matter and dark energy, in explaining a wide range of cosmological observations further undermines MOND’s viability.   So, is MOND “finished”? It’s hard to say definitively. Science rarely operates in absolutes, and theories are rarely “finished” in the sense of being completely discarded. Instead, they evolve, adapt, or fade into obscurity as new evidence emerges. For now, the weight of evidence seems to favor the dark matter paradigm, but MOND’s proponents may yet find ways to refine the theory or reconcile it with observations. Is the force of gravity instantaneous, or does it take time? The force of gravity is not instantaneous; it propagates at the speed of light. This is a consequence of general relativity, which describes gravity not as a force in the traditional Newtonian sense, but rather as the curvature of spacetime caused by the presence of mass and energy. Changes in the distribution of mass or energy—such as the movement of a massive object—result in ripples in spacetime known as gravitational waves. These waves carry information about the changes in the gravitational field and travel at the speed of light, c, the universal speed limit. This means that if, for example, the Sun were to suddenly vanish (ignoring the fact that this violates conservation laws), Earth would continue to orbit its former position for approximately 8.3 minutes—the time it takes for light to travel from the Sun to Earth—before "feeling" the absence of the Sun’s gravitational influence. This delay is a direct consequence of the finite speed at which gravity propagates. The notion of instantaneous gravitational interaction was a feature of Newton’s theory of gravitation, but it was superseded by Einstein’s more accurate framework. In general relativity, the concept of a gravitational "force" is replaced by the geometry of spacetime, and the dynamics of this geometry are governed by Einstein’s field equations, which inherently account for the finite speed of gravitational effects. This has been confirmed experimentally by the detection of gravitational waves by LIGO in 2015, which provided direct evidence that gravity does indeed propagate at the speed of light. Why do Hungarians change Budapest’s name as Bled Attila? Buda is like Hinduism and pest sounds unuseful/harmful animals. The name Budapest itself is a relatively modern construct, emerging in 1873 when the cities of Buda, Pest, and Óbuda were unified. The question of renaming it to "Bled Attila" seems to stem from a curious mix of linguistic playfulness and historical reinterpretation. Buda, derived from the name of the ancient Hun leader Bleda, brother of Attila the Hun, carries a deep historical resonance. Attila, a figure of mythic proportions in Hungarian lore, symbolizes strength and legacy, which might explain the appeal of incorporating his name into the city’s title. On the other hand, Pest, while now simply a part of the city’s name, originally referred to a "furnace" or "oven" in Slavic languages, likely due to the thermal springs in the area. It’s neither inherently harmful nor useless, but rather a functional descriptor of the region’s geography. The idea of renaming Budapest to "Bled Attila" appears to be more of a poetic reimagining than a practical proposal, blending historical homage with a touch of modern whimsy. Such a change, however, would require not only widespread cultural acceptance but also a redefinition of the city’s identity, which has long been tied to its current name. Ultimately, names are powerful symbols, and altering them is no trivial matter. Whether Budapest remains as it is or transforms into Bled Attila, the city’s essence lies not in its name but in the rich tapestry of its history, culture, and people. What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? The concept of "observation" in the double-slit experiment is often misunderstood, particularly when it comes to the role of intelligent creatures. In the context of quantum mechanics, an "observation" does not necessarily require a conscious observer. Instead, it refers to any interaction that causes the system to decohere, effectively collapsing the wavefunction and forcing the system into a definite state. This could be as simple as a photon interacting with a detector or even the environment itself. The key point is that the act of measurement—whether by a human, a machine, or the universe—disturbs the system in a way that reveals particle-like behavior.  Now, to the second part of the question: Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? The answer is nuanced. Light exhibits both wave-like and particle-like properties, and which one dominates depends on the experimental setup. In the double-slit experiment, if no measurement is made at the slits, light behaves as a wave, producing an interference pattern. However, if a measurement is made to determine which slit the photon passes through, the interference pattern disappears, and light behaves as a particle. This duality is intrinsic to quantum mechanics and is not contingent on the presence of an intelligent observer. The observer’s role is merely to facilitate the measurement process, not to "decide" the nature of light.  It’s worth noting that this duality is not unique to light. All quantum objects, from electrons to atoms, exhibit wave-particle duality. The double-slit experiment is a powerful demonstration of this principle, but it’s not the only one. The takeaway is that the nature of observation in quantum mechanics is deeply tied to the interaction between the system and its environment, not to the presence of consciousness or intelligence. Could gravitational redshift account for all cosmological redshift? If it includes all the matter inside the sphere between source and observer (radius)? Certainly not. Gravitational redshift occurs when light climbs out of a gravitational well, losing energy as it does so. But in the cosmological context, the redshifts we observe are not primarily due to local gravitational fields. Instead, they arise from the expansion of the universe itself—a stretching of spacetime. Even if you accounted for every speck of matter in a sphere between the source and observer, the gravitational redshift component would still be negligible compared to cosmological redshift on large scales.    Here’s why: First, gravitational redshift depends on the potential difference between emission and observation. But in a homogeneous universe, the net gravitational potential from matter inside such a sphere would largely cancel out due to symmetry—most contributions from distant matter pull equally in all directions. Second, cosmological redshift scales with distance in a way that gravitational redshift simply cannot. If you double the distance to a galaxy, the cosmological redshift roughly doubles (in the linear regime). Gravitational redshift, however, doesn’t accumulate linearly like that—it’s a local effect tied to specific potential wells, not an integrated property of expanding space.    What’s more, gravitational redshift can’t explain the observed uniformity of redshift-distance relations across different directions. If it were the dominant mechanism, we’d expect significant anisotropies or deviations based on local matter distributions. Instead, the smooth Hubble flow points unambiguously to expansion as the primary driver. Even galaxy clusters, where gravitational redshifts can be measured internally, show cosmological redshifts superimposed on top, not replaced by them.    Could there be corner cases where gravitational redshift mimics cosmological redshift? Maybe—if you painstakingly arranged matter in some contrived, finely-tuned shell structure. But nature doesn’t do fine-tuning for our convenience. The universe isn’t a nested set of perfect hollow spheres.
